requirements.requirement: Three-member etcd cluster running across node1/node2/node3 holding application keys
requirements.summary: etcd installed and configured on all three nodes with a static bootstrap; cluster formed with 3 started members (member list shows node1/node2/node3); 4 application keys under /app/ written via node1 endpoint and read back identically from node1, node2, and node3 endpoints, confirming replication across all three.

requirements.requirement: node3 member is permanently lost (data unrecoverable) while cluster quorum is preserved on the remaining members
requirements.summary: node3's etcd service was stopped and its data directory deleted, simulating permanent, unrecoverable loss. Endpoint health checked from node1 immediately afterward shows node1 and node2 healthy while node3's endpoint is unreachable/unhealthy, directly demonstrating quorum was preserved on the two surviving members during the disruption.

requirements.requirement: Dead node3 member is removed from the cluster and existing application keys remain intact under reduced (2-member) quorum
requirements.summary: etcdctl member remove against the dead member ID succeeded; the resulting member list shows only node1 and node2; a subsequent get --prefix on /app confirms all 4 application keys are still present and correct.

requirements.requirement: A new working etcd member is added and started on node3 (same system), restoring the cluster to 3 healthy members with the existing keys intact
requirements.summary: A new member was added via etcdctl member add (new member ID f0aa8b57251b972d, distinct from the destroyed member's ID), node3's local config was updated to ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=existing, and etcd was started and became active. Post-join checks show cluster-wide endpoint health healthy on all three endpoints, member list shows 3 started members (node1, node2, node3 with the new ID), and a direct get --prefix against node3's own endpoint returns all 4 original application keys unchanged.

requirements.requirement: (Independent) Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node with pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: All three nodes were rebooted sequentially. For each, a pre-reboot boot_id and healthy etcd/key state was captured, systemctl reboot was issued, the node was confirmed unreachable during the transition (connection refused/reset/timeout), a new boot_id was observed post-reboot (node1: dfeb3b70→39275521; node2: 28ae5f98→23ca7463; node3: bdd5de93→1d7386d7, matching the fixed global before/after-executor snapshots), and post-reboot checks confirmed etcd active, cluster-wide health, correct 3-member membership (including the new node3 member ID), and all 4 application keys intact.

overall_summary: The executor built the required 3-member etcd cluster (etcd was not pre-installed), loaded 4 application keys, then faithfully simulated the permanent loss of the node3 member (service stop + data directory deletion) while demonstrating quorum was preserved on node1/node2. It removed the dead member, added a fresh member on node3 with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=existing, and directly verified the cluster returned to 3 healthy members with all original keys present, including a read directly against node3's own endpoint. All observed member IDs, health, and key checks are internally consistent across the timeline and the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed correctly for all three nodes, with matching boot-identity changes cross-checked against the global before/after-executor snapshots and full cluster/key recovery confirmed after each reboot.
limitations: The 'permanent loss' of node3 was simulated by the executor rather than encountered as a pre-existing failure, since the environment started with no etcd installed at all; this is a reasonable executor-driven reconstruction of the stated scenario but means the loss and recovery were not independently, adversarially injected.

The /etc/hosts appends on all three nodes appear unused by the final etcd configuration (which relies on raw IPs), so their necessity could not be confirmed from the evidence; they are low-risk and were not reverted.

The prepare phase was disabled (before_prepare == after_prepare alias), so no preparer-created state exists to separate from executor changes; all changes seen in the executor_comparison are attributable to the executor.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands map cleanly to the task: apt install, config write, cluster bootstrap, key writes, simulated loss, member remove/add, and restart-protocol reboots each serve a clear purpose with no abandoned residue. One low-risk item stands out: on all three nodes the executor appended CLUSTER_HOSTS lines (node1/node2/node3 -> IPs) to /etc/hosts (cmd-7cd78a2a7d284bb8, cmd-c87df31ae63a4d95, cmd-c9265691d0574945), but the actual etcd configuration written afterward (cmd-25852bc42a3440fb, cmd-673eabd571894584, cmd-41387ae140a24bc3) uses raw IP addresses for all peer/client/advertise URLs, not hostnames, so this mutation had no demonstrated causal role in achieving the cluster outcome. It is bounded, additive, non-destructive, and left as a static file edit rather than a service-affecting change, so it is treated as a minor, low-severity unnecessary mutation rather than a serious hygiene issue. The one failed etcd start on node1 (cmd-9f693812288e4d6b, timeout) was a transient/self-resolved condition, not a lingering failure: the subsequent status check (cmd-4da7bcebe9a04c7e) and after_executor snapshot show etcd active with no failed systemd units on any node. Post-task global snapshots show no failed services, expected package-manager health, and only the intended etcd/ssh/dns sockets listening on all three nodes.
